cards.title: Optimal mixing of global Kawasaki dynamics on bounded-degree graphs
cards.formal: Fix an integer Δ≥3, inverse temperature β≥0 and magnetization η∈[−1,1]. If β<β_u(Δ), or if β>β_u(Δ) and |η|>η_a(Δ,β), must the global Kawasaki dynamics for the fixed-magnetization ferromagnetic Ising model mix in O(n log n) discrete updates on every n-vertex graph of maximum degree at most Δ? The implicit constant may depend on the fixed Δ,β,η, but not on n or the graph.
cards.why: Would identify the sharp update-count scale for constrained Ising sampling throughout the source’s fast-mixing regime on arbitrary bounded-degree graphs.
cards.status_note: The 2024 conference paper and final 2025 journal version checked, with later-result searches through 12 September 2026. Conjecture 1.4 remains explicit in the final version; no subsequent resolution of this all-graphs O(n log n) target was located.

progress.text: The source proves an O(n²) upper bound and conjectures O(n log n) for global Kawasaki dynamics in this regime.
The final published version retains the conjecture as Conjecture 1.4 and proves that the analytic and uniqueness thresholds need not coincide.

cards.definitions: For a finite undirected simple graph G=(V,E), n=|V|, put k=⌊n(1+η)/2⌋ and Ω_k={σ∈{−1,+1}^V: |{v:σ_v=+1}|=k}. Let m_G(σ) count edges with equal endpoint spins, and let μ̂(σ)=exp(βm_G(σ))/Σ_{τ∈Ω_k}exp(βm_G(τ)). One global Kawasaki step chooses a uniformly random +1 vertex u and a uniformly random −1 vertex v, proposes exchanging their spins, and accepts with probability min{1,exp(β[m_G(σ′)−m_G(σ)])}; otherwise it stays at σ. The vertices need not be adjacent. For k=0 or n the chain has one state. With transition matrix P, τ_mix is the least integer s with max_{σ∈Ω_k}(1/2)Σ_τ|P^s(σ,τ)−μ̂(τ)|≤1/4. The O(n log n) assertion is asymptotic: constants C,n_0 exist such that τ_mix≤Cn log n for all n≥n_0 and all such graphs. This avoids irrelevant very small periodic instances of the unmodified chain. In the source’s monochromatic-edge normalization, β_u(Δ)=ln(Δ/(Δ−2)). For β≥β_u, define Z_G^τ(β,z)=Σ_{σ consistent with τ}z^{|{v:σ_v=+1}|}exp(βm_G(σ)), where τ pins spins on any subset of vertices. The analytic threshold λ_a(Δ,β) is the smallest a≥1 such that for every compact D⊂(a,∞) there is δ>0 for which Z_G^τ(β,z)≠0 whenever |z−λ|<δ for some λ∈D, uniformly over all maximum-degree-Δ graphs and all pinnings τ. On the infinite Δ-regular tree, take the Ising Gibbs measure obtained as the limit of finite balls with all-plus boundary spins, edge weight exp(β·1[equal spins]) and activity λ per plus spin. Let η_a(Δ,β) be its expected root spin at λ=λ_a(Δ,β). The conjecture excludes β=β_u and the boundary |η|=η_a.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the uniform O(n log n) worst-start mixing bound for every fixed parameter triple in the stated regime, or refute it with an admissible fixed triple and a graph sequence whose mixing times exceed every constant multiple of n log n.

context_blocks.title: The total number of plus spins stays fixed
context_blocks.text: A usual single-site Ising update can change the magnetization. Kawasaki updates exchange opposite spins and therefore preserve exactly k plus spins. The target measure is the Ising measure conditioned on that count.

context_blocks.title: Global exchanges determine the time scale
context_blocks.text: A step can exchange distant vertices in any graph. Restricting exchanges to edges defines local Kawasaki dynamics, whose mixing can also be limited by transport across the graph. The conjecture concerns the global chain and counts one proposed exchange as one step.

context_blocks.title: Quadratic mixing is already known
context_blocks.text: The source proves O(n²) mixing in the indicated regime. The open strengthening reduces that worst-case bound to O(n log n); efficient sampling by another algorithm alone would not establish it.

context_blocks.title: The two thresholds must remain distinct
context_blocks.text: The analytic threshold uses zero-freeness under every pinning, while the tree uniqueness threshold asks for uniqueness of a Gibbs measure. The final 2025 version proves that these thresholds can differ. Replacing η_a by the smaller uniqueness-based threshold would change the conjecture.

cards.title: Deterministic divisibility testing by a constant-degree polynomial
cards.formal: For every fixed integer δ≥2, is there a deterministic algorithm using poly(n,s,d) arithmetic operations over Q that, given an explicitly s-sparse polynomial f∈Q[x_1,…,x_n] of total degree at most d and a nonzero polynomial g∈Q[x_1,…,x_n] of total degree at most δ, decides whether g divides f?
cards.why: Tests whether even a supplied low-degree factor of a sparse multivariate polynomial can be verified efficiently without randomness, a basic obstruction in deterministic factorization.
cards.status_note: Source field, cost model and missing predicate checked, together with the 2024 full-version record, the 2026 bounded-individual-degree result and arXiv:2606.12130 on finite-field sparse divisibility. The latter uses a different field and unrestricted divisor degrees. No resolution of this fixed-degree-divisor rational-arithmetic target was located through 12 September 2026.

progress.text: Forbes gives deterministic quasipolynomial-time divisibility testing for constant-degree divisors of sparse polynomials.
Dutta, Sinhababu and Thierauf retain polynomial-time testing as open even for quadratic divisors.
Chuyoon and Shpilka give new factorization guarantees under bounded individual degree of the dividend, while distinguishing the unrestricted case.

cards.definitions: A sparse representation of f lists its nonzero rational coefficients and corresponding nonnegative integer exponent vectors; s is the number of listed monomials and d bounds the sum of exponents in each monomial. The candidate divisor g is supplied by its coefficients and exponent vectors; because δ is fixed, it has at most binomial(n+δ,δ) monomials, so dense and sparse explicit encodings are polynomially related. Divisibility means that a polynomial h∈Q[x_1,…,x_n] exists with f=gh. The quotient need not be sparse and need not be output. The polynomial running-time exponent may depend on the fixed δ, but not on the input n,s,d. The source counts exact arithmetic operations over Q at unit cost. In particular, the requested bound is polynomial in the numerical degree d, not merely in log d, and is not a bound on rational-coefficient bit complexity. There is no promise that g is irreducible. The cases f=0 or nonzero constant g have immediate affirmative answers; the first unsettled divisor degree is two.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a deterministic divisibility decision algorithm with the stated polynomial arithmetic cost for every fixed δ, or establish an obstruction to that precise guarantee. Randomized testing, quasipolynomial time, or a bound requiring the dividend f to have constant individual degree does not answer the question.

context_blocks.title: The candidate factor is part of the input
context_blocks.text: This problem verifies one supplied potential divisor. It does not ask to discover all irreducible factors or to decide whether f itself is irreducible. The nonlinear candidate can already be quadratic.

context_blocks.title: A short polynomial need not have a short quotient
context_blocks.text: For example, x^D−1 is sparse and divisible by x−1, but its quotient has D terms. Sparsity of f therefore gives no promise that a quotient has few monomials relative to the sparse input length.

context_blocks.title: The known running time leaves a gap
context_blocks.text: Deterministic polynomial-time testing is available for linear divisors; for arbitrary fixed-degree nonlinear divisors, the cited general sparse-dividend result is quasipolynomial. The target removes that quasipolynomial overhead.

context_blocks.title: Recent bounded-individual-degree factoring is a different guarantee
context_blocks.text: The 2026 result gives polynomial time when every variable’s degree in the dividend is a fixed constant. Here only the divisor g has fixed total degree: the dividend can have arbitrarily large individual degrees up to d.

meta.status_scope: No claim of exhaustive open-status verification
methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. We aim for benchmarks of 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. All three use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The possible 1,000-problem expansion has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Deleted records are absent from the catalogue and exports. Their stable IDs and reasons are retained to prevent reimport. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The targets are 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. Top 100, Top 500 and the possible Top 1000 use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Records marked resolved are placed after the remaining candidates, without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.
